# Discovery Call Notes - National Horticultural Traders Association

## Call details

Call date: 2026-09-08.
Attendees: Executive Director, Membership Coordinator (National Horticultural Traders Association); Engagement Manager (delivery partner).
This was a first exploratory call, not a formal RFP; the association does not have a written requirements document yet.
The Executive Director opened by saying "we just know our current member experience feels dated and we want something modern with some AI in it."

## Organisation context

The National Horticultural Traders Association is a trade membership body for wholesale nurseries, garden retailers and landscape suppliers.
Members currently manage their profile, pay dues and browse the member directory through an old membership portal that the Executive Director could not name precisely, only saying "it might be called MemberSuite, or something similar, our office manager set it up years ago."
The Membership Coordinator said renewals are currently tracked "mostly by email and a shared spreadsheet, if I am honest."
Nobody on the call could say how many active members the association currently has; the Executive Director guessed "somewhere between a couple thousand and maybe five thousand, but I would need to check with finance."
The association's fiscal year runs January to December and dues renewals are meant to happen annually, though the Membership Coordinator admitted "a lot of members just let it lapse and we chase them later."

## What they are looking for

They want a modern member app that lets members log in, update their profile and renew their membership online.
They want some kind of AI feature but were not specific; the Executive Director said "maybe a chatbot that can answer member questions, or something that helps us write newsletters, we are open to ideas."
The Membership Coordinator would like members to be able to search the directory of other members more easily than today.
They mentioned wanting event registration for their annual trade show but were not sure if that should be part of this project or handled separately.
They would like renewal reminders to go out automatically instead of the Membership Coordinator tracking them manually.

## Things nobody could answer on the call

The Executive Director could not confirm how many members would actually use the new app versus staying on email and phone.
Nobody could say whether they have a target launch date; the Executive Director said only "sometime next year would be nice, but there is no hard deadline that I know of."
It is unclear which systems, if any, the new app would need to connect to beyond "whatever we are using for dues payments right now," which nobody on the call could name with certainty.
Nobody mentioned how many environments (development, testing, production) they would expect or currently have, and it was not asked.
No compliance or data-protection requirements were mentioned; when asked in passing whether they handle payment card data directly, the Executive Director said "I honestly am not sure, I think our current vendor handles that part."
Nobody expressed a cloud platform preference; the Executive Director said "we do not really have technical staff, so whatever you all think is best."
No budget range was discussed on this call; the Executive Director said pricing would be a separate conversation once they understand what is possible.
It is unclear whether the association wants a mobile app, a responsive website, or both.
Nobody could say whether any existing single sign-on or shared login system should be reused, since the association does not appear to have one today.

## Loosely stated requirements

The Executive Director said the new experience "should probably let members pay their dues online without calling the office."
The Membership Coordinator said it "would be nice" if members could see other members in their region or trade category.
The Executive Director said the chatbot idea "should only answer basic questions and not make anything up," but did not describe what a basic question looks like.
Both attendees agreed the current member directory search is frustrating but could not describe specifically what makes it hard to use.
The Executive Director mentioned they might want board members to have some kind of special access to reports, but was not able to describe what those reports would contain.

## Additional colour from the call

The Executive Director mentioned the board approved "some money" for this project at a recent meeting but did not state a figure or say whether it covers build, licensing or both.
The Membership Coordinator said a handful of members have emailed asking "why can't I just update my address myself" which is part of why this came up now.
Neither attendee could say whether the existing membership portal has an API or any way to export data; the Executive Director said "I genuinely do not know, that is a good question for our office manager."
The Executive Director said the association has about six staff in total and none of them are technical, so day-to-day support after launch would likely need to sit with the delivery partner or a future hire.
When asked about competitors or peer associations with a similar app, the Membership Coordinator mentioned "a couple of other trade groups have something like this" but could not name them or describe what they liked about those apps.
The call ended with the Executive Director asking "what would you even need from us to give us a rough idea of cost," which the Engagement Manager said would be the subject of a follow-up call once open items are resolved.

## What happens next

The delivery partner will send a short list of clarifying questions covering member count, systems, timeline and budget before any proposal can be drafted.
The Executive Director agreed to loop in the office manager, who set up the original membership portal, for the next call.
The Membership Coordinator agreed to check whether finance can produce an approximate current member count before the next call.
No commitments were made on scope, timeline or cost during this call; everything discussed here is directional only.

## Follow-ups the delivery partner needs from the customer

Confirm the actual current member count and the platform name and vendor for the existing membership system.
Confirm whether event registration for the annual trade show is in scope for this engagement or a separate future project.
Confirm whether the association directly handles payment card data or whether an existing payment vendor is fully responsible for that.
Confirm whether there is any target date, even an approximate one, and any budget range the association has in mind.
Confirm who on the association's side, if anyone, can act as a technical or business point of contact once the project starts.
Confirm whether the existing membership portal exposes any API or export mechanism that a new app could build on.

prd.title: Member Experience Modernisation - Product Requirements Document

statements.text: The National Horticultural Traders Association wants a modern member app with an unspecified AI feature, but this first exploratory call left member count, launch date, environments, integration details, compliance scope, cloud preference and budget all unconfirmed; confidence is low until these gaps are closed with the customer.
statements.label: ai-interpretation

statements.text: Member Experience Modernisation serves 3 business objectives set by National Horticultural Traders Association (BR_01, BR_02 and BR_03); each is detailed under Business objectives.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: The solution is organised into 3 capability areas (Application Experience, Platform Foundation and AI Capabilities) and names no existing system to connect to.
statements.label: ai-interpretation

statements.text: Today National Horticultural Traders Association relies on Existing Membership Portal (Unconfirmed Platform): An old membership portal is in use today; even its product name is uncertain, possibly "MemberSuite," set up years ago by an office manager.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: Until this is addressed, National Horticultural Traders Association cannot achieve "Modernise a dated member experience" (BR_01), "Member self-service demand signal" (BR_02) and "Automate renewal reminders" (BR_03).
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: BR_01 - Modernise a dated member experience: The association wants a modern member experience with some AI capability, replacing a portal staff describe as dated.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: BR_02 - Member self-service demand signal: Members have emailed asking to update their own contact details directly, evidencing demand for self-service.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: BR_03 - Automate renewal reminders: The association wants renewal reminders to go out automatically instead of being tracked manually by the Membership Coordinator.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: PER_01 - Member: A representative of a member business (a wholesale nursery, garden retailer or landscape supplier) who logs in, updates the business profile and renews membership.

statements.text: PER_02 - Association Staff (Non-Technical): The association's roughly six staff, none technical, who will need to operate and support the app after launch.

summary.text: The proposed solution architecture targets Google Cloud Platform (GCP) and is composed of 19 components covering 9 functional capabilities. It spans the full reviewed scope; see each component’s own rationale below for its specific citations.
summary.label: ai-interpretation

summary.text: Mobile Backend is not proposed yet because GAP_08 (Mobile app vs. website undecided) is unresolved; add it once that gap is closed.
summary.label: assumption-to-confirm

components.name: Web Front End
components.purpose: Serves the customer-facing web experience and delivers static assets close to users.
components.rationale: Firebase Hosting (global CDN) serves the web experience with edge caching, TLS termination and low first-byte latency worldwide. It addresses BR_02.
tradeOffs: Edge caching improves latency but requires explicit cache-invalidation on release.
A globally distributed edge adds a small recurring data-transfer cost versus single-region hosting.
securityConsiderations: Enforce HTTPS-only delivery and a strict Content-Security-Policy at the edge.
Restrict direct access to origin storage so all traffic is served through the CDN.

components.name: API Layer
components.purpose: Exposes the solution's functional capabilities as versioned, governed APIs for the front end and integrations.
components.rationale: Apigee API Management centralizes authentication, throttling and request validation ahead of the application compute runtime. It addresses BR_02, BR_03, FR_01, FR_02, FR_03, FR_04, FR_05, FR_06, FR_08, FR_09, DATA_01 and DATA_02.
tradeOffs: A managed gateway adds a small per-request latency and cost overhead versus calling services directly.
API versioning policy must be agreed early to avoid breaking existing client integrations.
securityConsiderations: Apply request-rate throttling and payload-size limits to reduce abuse and denial-of-service exposure.
Validate and authorize every request against the identity provider before it reaches the runtime.

components.name: Application Compute Runtime
components.purpose: Hosts the backend business logic that implements the reviewed functional requirements.
components.rationale: Google Cloud Run runs the backend services with managed autoscaling so capacity tracks real traffic without manual intervention. It addresses FR_01, FR_06 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: Container-based hosting requires a build/release pipeline for every deployable service.
Autoscaling limits must be tuned against real traffic before go-live to avoid cost or latency surprises.
securityConsiderations: Run containers with least-privilege service identities and no long-lived static credentials.
Scan container images for known vulnerabilities before each release.

components.name: Primary Relational Database
components.purpose: Stores the core transactional data the application reads and writes.
components.rationale: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL provides managed relational storage with automated backups, patching and encryption at rest. It addresses DATA_01 and DATA_02.
tradeOffs: A managed relational engine caps vertical scale; very high write throughput may need read replicas or partitioning later.
Schema migrations must be coordinated with application deployments to avoid downtime.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt data at rest and in transit, and restrict network access to the application tier only.
Apply least-privilege database roles per service rather than a single shared credential.

components.name: Customer Identity and Access Management
components.purpose: Handles registration, sign-in, session management and multi-factor authentication for end users.
components.rationale: Identity Platform provides managed sign-up, sign-in, SSO federation and MFA so authentication is never implemented by hand. It addresses FR_01, FR_06 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: A managed identity provider constrains custom sign-in UX to its supported customization hooks.
Federating with an external identity provider (SSO) adds a dependency on that provider’s availability.
securityConsiderations: Enforce MFA for privileged accounts and require strong password/session policies for all users.
Log every authentication and authorization decision for audit purposes.

components.name: Monitoring
components.purpose: Tracks infrastructure and application health so incidents are detected before customers report them.
components.rationale: Cloud Monitoring aggregates metrics and dashboards with alerting thresholds tied to the availability and performance targets. It addresses FR_01, FR_06 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: Alert thresholds must be tuned to avoid both alert fatigue and missed incidents.
Detailed metric retention adds a recurring storage cost proportional to system scale.
securityConsiderations: Restrict dashboard and alert access to operations and engineering roles only.

components.name: Centralized Logging
components.purpose: Centralizes application and infrastructure logs for troubleshooting and audit.
components.rationale: Cloud Logging aggregates structured logs from every service with a defined, policy-driven retention period. It addresses FR_01, FR_06 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: Centralized log retention has a direct storage cost that scales with request volume.
Log content must be scrubbed of personal or sensitive data before it is retained.
securityConsiderations: Redact personal or sensitive data from log payloads before they are written.
Restrict log access to authorized operations staff and retain an access audit trail.

components.name: CI/CD Pipeline
components.purpose: Automates build, test and release of every service into each environment.
components.rationale: Cloud Build with Cloud Deploy runs the build/test/release pipeline consistently across development, test and production. It addresses CON_01.
tradeOffs: A fully automated pipeline needs an initial investment in test coverage to be trustworthy for production releases.
securityConsiderations: Require code review and passing automated security scans before a release can be promoted.
Keep deployment credentials scoped to the pipeline identity, never to individual engineers.

components.name: Infrastructure as Code
components.purpose: Defines every environment declaratively so dev/test/prod stay reproducible and auditable.
components.rationale: Google Cloud Infrastructure Manager provisions and updates cloud resources declaratively, so environment drift is detected instead of accumulating silently. It addresses CON_01.
tradeOffs: Declarative provisioning has a learning curve for teams used to manual console changes.
securityConsiderations: Store infrastructure state and variables in a controlled, access-audited location, never in source control in plain text.

components.name: Secrets Manager
components.purpose: Stores and rotates credentials, API keys and connection strings used by every service.
components.rationale: Secret Manager centralizes credential storage with automatic rotation and fine-grained access policies. It addresses FR_01, FR_06 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: Every service must be updated to fetch secrets at runtime rather than reading them from local configuration.
securityConsiderations: Grant read access to a secret only to the specific service identities that need it.
Rotate credentials on a defined schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure.

components.name: Key Management
components.purpose: Manages the encryption keys that protect data at rest across storage and database services.
components.rationale: Cloud KMS issues and rotates encryption keys with a full audit trail of every key-use event. It addresses FR_01, FR_06 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: Customer-managed keys add operational responsibility for key rotation and recovery policy.
securityConsiderations: Rotate keys on a defined schedule and restrict key administration to a small, audited group.

components.name: Backup
components.service: Google Cloud Backup and DR Service
components.purpose: Protects stored data with policy-driven, regularly tested backups.
components.rationale: Google Cloud Backup and DR Service takes policy-driven, encrypted backups on a defined schedule with a tested restore procedure. It addresses FR_01, FR_06 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: Backup retention has a direct storage cost that scales with data volume and retention period.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt backups at rest and test restores on a regular schedule, not only after an incident.

components.name: Network Protection
components.service: VPC Service Controls with Private Service Connect
components.purpose: Isolates backend services on a private network so they are not directly reachable from the public internet.
components.rationale: VPC Service Controls with Private Service Connect keeps service-to-service traffic off the public internet and restricts inbound access to approved paths only. It addresses FR_01, FR_06 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: Private networking adds configuration overhead when a new service or integration needs external connectivity.
securityConsiderations: Default to deny-all network rules and open only the specific paths a service requires.
Log and periodically review network access-control changes.

components.name: WAF / DDoS Protection
components.purpose: Filters malicious inbound traffic and absorbs volumetric attacks at the edge, in front of the public entry point.
components.rationale: Google Cloud Armor inspects inbound requests against managed and custom rule sets and mitigates volumetric attacks before they reach the application. It addresses FR_01, FR_06 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: Rule tuning is required to avoid false positives blocking legitimate traffic.
securityConsiderations: Enable managed rule sets for common web exploits and review blocked-request logs regularly.
Alert on traffic patterns consistent with a volumetric or application-layer attack.

components.name: Data Warehouse
components.purpose: Provides a column-oriented analytical store for cross-domain reporting and analysis.
components.rationale: BigQuery holds curated, query-optimized data separate from transactional load so reporting never competes with production traffic. It addresses FR_08.
tradeOffs: A separate analytical store adds pipeline latency between an event occurring and it being reportable.

The driving requirement is Low-priority and not yet fully defined; a small set of reporting views directly in the primary relational database would be sufficient until it is confirmed, rather than committing to this component now.
securityConsiderations: Apply row/column-level access controls so analysts see only the data domains they are authorized for.

components.name: BI / Reporting
components.purpose: Delivers self-service dashboards and reports to business stakeholders over the warehouse.
components.rationale: Looker provides governed, self-service dashboards over curated warehouse data. It addresses FR_08.
tradeOffs: Self-service reporting requires a governed semantic layer to prevent conflicting metric definitions.

The driving requirement is Low-priority and not yet fully defined; scheduled exports or database-backed reporting views instead of a dedicated BI platform would be sufficient until it is confirmed, rather than committing to this component now.
securityConsiderations: Scope dashboard access by role so stakeholders see only their authorized data domains.

components.name: LLM Platform
components.purpose: Provides managed access to foundation models for the AI use cases identified in the reviewed scope.
components.rationale: Vertex AI (Generative AI / Model Garden) gives managed, guardrailed access to foundation models so AI functionality is not built on an unmanaged model endpoint. It addresses FR_02 and FR_07.
tradeOffs: Model responses are probabilistic; outputs affecting decisions need a human-review step (see AI solution approach).
securityConsiderations: Apply content-safety guardrails and never send unmasked personal data in a prompt without a documented basis.

components.name: Search Service
components.purpose: Provides fast, relevant search and discovery over application content.
components.rationale: Vertex AI Search indexes application content for fast, relevance-ranked search rather than relying on database queries. It addresses FR_03 and FR_09.
tradeOffs: A dedicated search index must be kept synchronized with the source of truth, adding a small propagation delay.

The driving requirement is Low-priority and not yet fully defined; database-backed filtering and sorting instead of a dedicated search index would be sufficient until it is confirmed, rather than committing to this component now.
securityConsiderations: Apply the same authorization filters to search results as to direct data access, so search cannot leak restricted content.

components.name: Notification Service
components.service: Firebase Cloud Messaging with Pub/Sub-triggered email/SMS delivery
components.purpose: Delivers email, SMS and push notifications and alerts to end users.
components.rationale: Firebase Cloud Messaging with Pub/Sub-triggered email/SMS delivery delivers multi-channel notifications with delivery tracking, separate from the transactional data path. It addresses BR_03 and FR_05.
tradeOffs: Delivery across third-party email/SMS/push channels is subject to those channels’ own rate and deliverability limits.
securityConsiderations: Honor user opt-out/consent preferences and avoid placing sensitive personal data in notification payloads.

environments.purpose: Feature development and integration testing for engineers before promotion.
environments.sizing: Matches the production topology at reduced instance/node counts. Environment count is not configured, so this is an assumption pending confirmation.

environments.purpose: Functional, regression and non-functional test execution prior to release.
environments.sizing: Matches the production topology at reduced instance/node counts. Environment count is not configured, so this is an assumption pending confirmation.

environments.sizing: Sized for the expected user volume once confirmed, with autoscaling enabled. Environment count is not configured, so this is an assumption pending confirmation.

useCases.retrieval: Answers are grounded in National Horticultural Traders Association's own indexed content: the assistant retrieves the top-matching passages before generating a response and cites the source passage instead of answering from the model's general training data. Retrieval runs against Vertex AI (Generative AI / Model Garden).
useCases.orchestration: A stateful workflow retrieves context, drafts an answer, checks the draft against the retrieved passages for groundedness, and only then returns it to the "Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant: AI feature - concept only and 1 related function" user, so an ungrounded draft never reaches them.
useCases.evaluation: A golden set of representative questions with expected answers runs on every prompt or model change; groundedness (does the answer match the retrieved passage) and answer relevance are scored automatically, and the regression suite blocks release on a drop.
useCases.safety: Prompt-injection defences separate retrieved content from the system prompt, content filters run on every response, and abnormal request volume or repeated jailbreak attempts are flagged for abuse review.
useCases.privacy: Only the minimum personal data needed to answer is included in the prompt context, requests are processed within United States (unspecified), and the provider's terms exclude request content from model training.
useCases.humanReview: The assistant answers informational questions only; any answer touching a binding decision is withheld and routed to a human, and every answer links back to its source document for verification.
useCases.monitoring: Request volume, latency, token cost, error rate and the evaluation score trend are tracked in Cloud Monitoring, Cloud Logging, with an alert when the evaluation score or error rate crosses its threshold.

data.architecturePattern: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant, orchestrated with LangGraph and served behind the platform's managed AI service.

frameworks.name: LangGraph
frameworks.rationale: The reviewed AI scope (FR_02, FR_07, Q_13) needs a stateful, multi-step workflow - retrieval/generation with a groundedness check, or several coordinated use cases - with an explicit human-in-the-loop checkpoint before a result is acted on; LangGraph models that as a graph of steps with durable state, which a single prompt call cannot provide.
alternatives: A single prompt call per request (insufficient: it cannot hold state across the retrieve/draft/check steps or pause for human review).
LangChain agents without a graph (workable, but its implicit control flow is harder to audit for the required human-checkpoint than an explicit LangGraph state machine).

frameworks.name: Vercel AI SDK
frameworks.rationale: No .NET or Java preference is stated, so the front end streams model output using the same TypeScript stack as the rest of the application (FR_02, FR_07, Q_13); the Vercel AI SDK's streaming hooks remove the need to hand-roll server-sent-event/token-streaming handling in the UI.
alternatives: Mastra (a comparable TypeScript agent/streaming SDK; either is suitable, Vercel AI SDK is preferred for its more direct React streaming hooks).

frameworks.name: Vertex AI (Generative AI / Model Garden)
frameworks.rationale: Hosting the model(s) for FR_02, FR_07, Q_13 on Vertex AI (Generative AI / Model Garden) keeps inference inside the Google Cloud Platform account boundary already used for the rest of the solution, avoiding a separate vendor contract, network egress path and access-control model to operate.
alternatives: A self-hosted open-weight model on Kubernetes/GPU nodes (higher operational overhead; only justified by a strict data-residency or cost-at-scale constraint the reviewed scope does not state).

data.promptManagement: Each use case's (Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant: AI feature - concept only and 1 related function) system and user prompts are versioned in source control next to the code that calls them, changed only through code review, and re-run against that use case's golden set in CI before the change ships; the model's JSON output is validated against a versioned JSON schema for that use case, so a malformed response is rejected rather than passed downstream.
data.evaluationApproach: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant: AI feature - concept only and 1 related function: A golden set of representative questions with expected answers runs on every prompt or model change; groundedness (does the answer match the retrieved passage) and answer relevance are scored automatically, and the regression suite blocks release on a drop.

Each driver cites the reviewed requirements, capabilities, architecture components, integrations or AI use cases that justify it, and its complexity is derived from the facts named in its rationale. The main complexity hotspots are Cloud platform foundation and environments (DRV_08), Existing Membership Portal (Unconfirmed Platform) Connectivity (DRV_10) and Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant: AI feature - concept only and 1 related function (DRV_13). No capability in the functional scope is dedicated to security, so security and compliance controls are estimated as their own workstream from the reviewed security-related requirements. rules.name: Driver effort
rules.formula: driver days = baseEffort[driver type][complexity]; complexity = reviewer override ?? AI suggestion
rules.description: Each scope driver is sized from the editable base-effort table. The AI only suggests the complexity level; a reviewer override replaces it and is marked user-set. A driver without a base-effort value contributes no days, is reported as a blocked scope driver and blocks the cost of its workstream and the ROM.

rules.name: Workstream base effort and complexity
rules.formula: base days = sum(driver days); complexity = round(sum(level x driver days) / sum(driver days)), Low = 1 ... Very High = 4
rules.description: A workstream is the sum of its drivers. Its complexity is the effort-weighted average of the driver complexity levels.

rules.name: Environment uplift
rules.formula: infrastructure days x (1 + max(0, environments - baselineEnvironments) x extraEnvironmentPct / 100)
rules.description: Environments beyond the baseline add effort to infrastructure drivers only. When the number of environments is unknown, no uplift is applied, the input is listed as missing and confidence is reduced.

rules.name: Productivity factor
rules.formula: likely days = round((non-infrastructure days + uplifted infrastructure days) x productivityFactor)
rules.description: The productivity assumption scales all build effort (below 1 is faster than baseline). Likely effort is rounded to whole days.

rules.name: Overhead phases
rules.formula: phase days = round(total likely build days x pctOfBuild / 100)
rules.description: Discovery and Architecture, Testing and Hardening, and Deployment and Handover are sized as configurable percentages of the adjusted build effort and staffed with the overhead role mix.

rules.name: Workstream confidence
rules.formula: High -> Medium (Very High driver, related open gap or question, outstanding delivery dependency, missing planning input) -> Low (critical unresolved gap or question on an affected input, or a blocked calculation)
rules.description: Inputs map to workstreams by driver type: integration readiness -> integration, data volume -> data, AI data availability -> AI, expected users / environments / target regions -> infrastructure, compliance scope -> security, delivery deadline -> timeline. Every reduction is listed as a confidence limitation. Overhead phases inherit the overall confidence.

rules.name: Overall confidence
rules.formula: Low if any calculation is blocked, Low-confidence workstreams hold >= 30% of build effort, or 4 or more distinct estimation inputs are missing; Medium if any workstream is below High or any input is missing; else High
rules.description: The overall level is weighted by effort so that one small uncertain workstream does not dominate, while blocked calculations and a largely unspecified engagement always do.

rules.name: Effort range
rules.formula: low = round(likely x (1 - lowPct / 100)); high = round(likely x (1 + highPct / 100))
rules.description: The range width comes from the confidence-spread table, so lower confidence widens the range instead of presenting unsupported precision. Totals are the sums of the workstream ranges.

rules.name: Role allocation
rules.formula: role days = likely days x sum(driver-type days x role mix share) / sum(driver-type days), in tenths of a day (largest remainder)
rules.description: Likely effort is split across roles with the role mix of each driver type, weighted by that type's days. Role days always add up exactly to the likely effort.

rules.name: Workstream cost
rules.formula: cost = sum(role days x role day rate); range = cost x (1 - lowPct / 100) .. cost x (1 + highPct / 100)
rules.description: A role with allocated days but no day rate, effort without a role mix, or a driver without base effort blocks the workstream cost and the ROM totals. No default rate is ever substituted.

rules.name: ROM commercials
rules.formula: subtotal = roundToUnit(sum(workstream cost)); contingency = roundToUnit(subtotal x contingencyPct / 100); ROM = subtotal + contingency
rules.description: Low, likely and high values are each rounded to the configured rounding unit and reported in the configured currency.

rules.name: Timeline
rules.formula: capacity = teamSize x workingDaysPerWeek; weeks = ceil(effort / capacity); build window = ceil(sum(build phase effort) / capacity)
rules.description: Discovery runs first; the build phases run concurrently and share the team; Testing and Hardening may overlap the last 25% of the build window but always keeps at least one week after it; Deployment and Handover runs last. The range applies the timeline confidence spread, rounded up to whole weeks.

rules.name: Deadline assessment
rules.formula: compare likely and high timeline weeks with deliveryDeadlineWeeks; required team = smallest team size whose likely timeline <= deadline
rules.description: When no deadline is configured the assessment says so, the deadline is listed as a missing input and timeline confidence is reduced.

rules.name: Missing inputs
rules.formula: missing planning input -> confidence reduced; missing day rate, role mix or base effort -> calculation blocked
rules.description: Each missing input names the affected workstreams or estimate components, the related scope items and how to resolve it. An input held open by a gap or question is never dropped: without a workstream of its driver type it affects the workstreams that share requirements with the open item, otherwise the overall estimate.
